title: Bulk RFID Cards — Volume Pricing, 1K to 1M+
summary: Proud Tek is a direct RFID card factory in Shenzhen — running since 2008 and shipping to B2B buyers worldwide — built for volume: order blank or fully printed, encoded RFID cards in bulk and the per-card price drops 25-40% below small-order rates as the run deepens. This page is written for the volume buyer, not the RFID beginner: where the quantity breaks sit (1K, 5K, 10K, 50K, 100K and 500K+), what actually moves the per-card cost, how batch QC and 100% functional testing hold at six-figure quantities, the air-versus-sea freight math on a pallet of cards, and the blanket-order and scheduled call-off programs that keep a multi-year card supply predictable. For chip selection and per-SKU detail, follow the card links below.
heroPoints: Volume pricing that actually moves — per-card cost steps down at the 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K, 100K and 500K+ quantity breaks, with the deepest rates reserved for annual and blanket-order supply agreements, all quoted per program rather than from a fixed list.

Blank stock and custom runs both ship in bulk — pre-laminated MIFARE Classic, MIFARE DESFire, NTAG 215, EM4100 and T5577 cards for 2-3 day dispatch, or full-colour printed, encoded and numbered cards on 5-7 day production for orders from 1,000 to 1,000,000+.
100% functional testing at any volume, 2-3% overage supplied at cost for field spares, and one production run held to one standard — so unit 1 and unit 100,000 read identically.

brief.label: What bulk buying gets you
brief.text: One factory production run at a locked spec: identical chip performance, print registration and lamination across the whole batch, pre-encoding done on the line at no extra per-card cost on volume orders, and one shipment through one customs clearance instead of repeat small orders all year.

brief.label: What counts as bulk
brief.text: Bulk starts at 1,000 cards, with price tiers at 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K, 100K and 500K+ pieces and the first major break around 10K. Mixed-chip orders share one run at a 500-piece minimum per chip type. Exact MOQ and pricing are quoted per program — there is no published price list.

brief.label: How pricing works at volume
brief.text: Quotes are itemised, not list-priced, because per-card cost turns on chip family, card material, finishing, encoding scope and order volume. As a public anchor: a card near $0.35 at 500 pieces runs about $0.12-$0.18 at 50,000 pieces factory-direct — indicative only, since every program is quoted on its own spec.

brief.label: Proof to pull first
brief.text: ISO 9001, ISO 14001 and ISO 45001 certificates (number and registrar on request), a 100% functional test report shipped with every lot, seven-year batch traceability, and per-shipment RoHS / REACH SVHC / Certificate-of-Conformity declarations — all verifiable before you commit.

sections.title: Why buy RFID cards in bulk direct from the factory
sections.intro: Bulk card buying is mostly about deleting repeated fixed costs. Set-up, plate-making, encoding configuration, QC documentation and freight all happen once per run regardless of quantity, so the more cards behind a single set-up, the less each one carries. A factory also holds one batch to one standard — something a buyer piecing stock together from several distributors never gets. Start with the [full RFID card range](/products/rfid-cards/), or line up the sourcing questions in the [wholesale RFID quote reading guide](/blog/rfid-tag-wholesale-quote-reading-guide/) and the [RFID RFP template](/blog/rfid-rfp-template-questions-suppliers/) before you ask for tiers.

dataHighlight.heading: Per card at 50,000 pieces
dataHighlight.text: A card near $0.35 at 500 pieces drops to about $0.12-$0.18 at 50,000 pieces factory-direct — thousands saved on a large deployment. Figures are indicative and quoted per program, never taken from a fixed list.

bullets: Per-unit cost drops hard at volume: a card near $0.35 at 500 pieces can run $0.12-$0.18 at 50,000 pieces factory-direct — a swing that funds the whole deployment, though the exact number is always quoted per program.
One run, one standard: identical chip performance, print registration and lamination across 100,000 cards instead of the mixed-source variation you get stitching together distributor stock.
Pre-encoding folded into production: UID sequences, NDEF records, sector keys or custom data written on the line at no extra per-card cost for basic encoding on volume orders.
Consolidated logistics: one production lot, one customs clearance and one receiving event instead of chasing repeat small orders through the year.
Annual supply agreements lock the deep-tier price and reserve production slots, insulating the program from material-cost swings and peak-season lead-time slips.

sections.title: Volume tiers and the card families you can run at scale
sections.intro: Almost any card in the catalogue runs at bulk volume; the families below are the ones procurement teams order at five- and six-figure quantities. The ladder is simple — each quantity break lowers the per-card cost — but the figure itself depends on the chip and finish, so we quote per program rather than publish a list you would have to caveat. Browse the parts on the [RFID cards pillar](/products/rfid-cards/).

bullets: 1,000 cards is the bulk floor — below it you are in sample and short-run pricing; above it the volume ladder starts.
The first major per-card break lands around 10,000 cards; 50K and 100K open deeper tiers; 500K+ and annual commitments earn the best rate — every figure quoted per program.
Mixed-chip orders share one run at a 500-piece minimum per chip type — for example 5,000 MIFARE Classic 1K and 3,000 MIFARE DESFire cards on one PO, each with its own artwork and encoding.

Every card runs to a published standard — ISO/IEC 7810 for the ID-1 (CR80) body, ISO/IEC 14443 for 13.56 MHz HF chips like MIFARE Classic and NTAG, and the 125 kHz LF air interface for EM and T5577 parts — so the credential outlives any single reader model.

sections.title: What moves the per-card price — factory run vs stitched-together stock
sections.intro: Bulk quotes are itemised, and each line reacts to volume differently. Knowing the cost structure lets you trade specification against budget on purpose instead of discovering the drivers after three rounds of quotes — and it is the clearest reason a single factory run beats piecing a large quantity together from distributor shelves.

comparePanel.beforeHeading: Piecing bulk cards together from distributors
before: Stock pulled from several lots — chip batch, print registration and lamination vary card to card.
You encode the cards yourself, or pay a separate bureau after they arrive.
Each distributor order clears customs and ships on its own, multiplying freight and handling.
Per-card price flattens fast — distributor margin sits on top of the factory price at every tier.
No single owner for a defect that only shows up at 40,000 cards.
after: One chip lot and one set-up: identical RF performance and print across the entire batch.
Pre-encoding written on the line and 100% read-tested, at no extra per-card cost for basic encoding on volume.
One production lot, one customs clearance, one receiving event — freight quoted air and sea together.
Factory-direct pricing that keeps stepping down through 10K, 50K, 100K and 500K+ tiers, quoted per program.
A named account engineer owns the spec across reorders, with 2-3% overage supplied at cost for spares.

bullets: Chip family is the biggest single line: a legacy LF or MIFARE Classic chip costs a fraction of a MIFARE DESFire or NTAG 424 DNA, and chip allocation sets the floor at any volume.
Set-up and tooling amortise over the run: print plates, die-cut tooling and encoding configuration are fixed costs that spread thinner the deeper the order goes.
Card material moves the baseline: standard PVC is the volume default; PETG, polycarbonate, wood, bamboo and metal bodies each add material and process cost.
Finishing adds production passes: spot UV, hot-foil stamping, magnetic stripe, embossed numbering and signature panels are each priced per pass.
Encoding scope: basic UID read and NDEF write is included on volume orders; complex DESFire application setup or multi-sector keys carry a small per-card fee, quoted upfront.
Packaging variant: bulk poly bag is the volume default; individual sleeves, retail blister or branded boxes add per-unit packing cost.

sections.title: From free sample to cards delivered at volume — order, QC and logistics
sections.intro: Nobody should commit a six-figure card run to a design they have not held. The path below front-loads the cheap, reversible steps — a [free sample pack](/sample-pack/) first, a 100-piece pilot second, and a locked-price production run only once a first article is approved on your own reader. After that, QC and freight are the two levers that decide when the cards land; the [air-versus-sea freight trade-off](/blog/rfid-shipping-air-vs-sea-freight-cost-tradeoff/) is quoted on every bulk order.

image.alt: A five-step bulk card order flow, left to right. Step 1, free card samples: blanks plus a printed proof in 5-10 business days. Step 2, spec and quote: chip, artwork, encoding and quantity tiers confirmed in writing with an itemised MOQ ladder. Step 3, pilot and first article: a 100-piece pilot approved on your own reader, the decision gate. Step 4, volume run and QC: a 1,000 to 1,000,000-plus card run on 5-7 day production with 100% functional testing. Step 5, pack and deliver: air freight in 3-7 days or sea in 25-45 days, with scheduled call-off for blanket orders. A base arrow shows the order moving from free sample to delivered at volume.

items.label: 1. Free card samples
items.text: Tell us the card, chip and finish; we ship blanks plus a printed proof (FOB Shenzhen, typically 5-10 business days) so your team can test fit, print and read on the actual equipment.

items.label: 2. Spec & quote
items.text: We confirm chip, artwork, encoding scheme, packaging and the quantity tiers you want priced, then return an itemised quote with an MOQ ladder and both air and sea freight — nothing left implicit before tooling.

items.label: 3. Pilot & first article
items.text: A 100-piece pilot encoded with your real data, approved on your own reader or lock; the signed first article becomes the reference so unit 1 and unit 100,000 match.

items.label: 4. Volume run & 100% QC
items.text: Full run at locked pricing on 5-7 day production, every encoded card functional-tested at the line, out-of-spec lots quarantined, 2-3% overage supplied at cost for spares.

items.label: 5. Pack & deliver
items.text: Poly-bag, sleeve or branded-box packing to spec, then dispatch — express for pilots, air 3-7 days or sea 25-45 days for the balance, with scheduled call-off against blanket orders.

bullets: 100% functional testing: every encoded card is checked for chip response and read performance at the line; failures are rejected and replaced before packing.
First-piece and in-process control: first-piece QC at line start, then AQL sampling on visual and dimensional attributes, with out-of-spec lots quarantined before the next step.
Documented test report on the encoded lot ships in the box, with the encoding database where applicable; batches stay traceable by lot for seven years.

Freight is the other lever on landed cost: express courier 3-5 days for pilots, air 3-7 days at roughly $4-8/kg, sea LCL around $80-250 per cubic meter at 25-45 days, or FCL from roughly $1,500-4,500 for six-figure runs.
Split-mode on tight schedules: air-ship the urgent 10-20% so issuance starts on time and put the remaining 80-90% on the water, quoted together on FOB Shenzhen / Yantian or DDP terms.

sections.title: Proof your procurement team can verify
sections.intro: Trust on a first bulk order is not a feeling; it is a set of documents your supplier-qualification team can check independently. Everything below is verifiable before you commit — the [certifications page](/about/certifications/) lists each standard and how to confirm it with the registrar, and the [factory page](/about/factory/) documents the plant behind the numbers.
checklist: ISO 9001, ISO 14001 and ISO 45001 certificates — certificate number and issuing registrar provided on request for independent verification.
100% functional test on every encoded card, with the functional test report and encoding database delivered alongside the shipment.
First-article approval on your own reader or lock before the volume run, so a reader mismatch surfaces at pilot stage, not at card 40,000.
Per-shipment documentation pack: Certificate of Origin, Certificate of Conformity for radio compliance, and RoHS / REACH SVHC / Prop 65 material declarations by SKU.
Batch traceability by encoding lot with records retained seven years; quality claims within 30 days of receipt resolved by free replacement or proportional refund.
Open factory audits at our Shenzhen operation by appointment, plus virtual walk-throughs and third-party (SGS, TUV, Intertek) inspection when a program requires it.

callout.label: Ask for the evidence before you buy
callout.text: For a qualified program we share the functional-test yield, AQL inspection results and a pre-production sample for your shortlisted card SKUs as part of the sample pack — the same records our own QA signs off against.

faq.question: What is the minimum order (MOQ) for bulk RFID cards?
faq.answer: Bulk starts at 1,000 cards. Volume tiers step at 1K, 5K, 10K, 50K, 100K and 500K+ pieces, with the first major per-card break around 10K and the deepest rates on 100K+ annual commitments. Mixed-chip orders share one run at a 500-piece minimum per chip type. Exact MOQ depends on chip, material and encoding, so we quote it per program rather than post one number that would be wrong for half of them.

faq.question: How much cheaper is 100,000 cards than 10,000?
faq.answer: Per-card cost keeps stepping down as the run deepens, but the size of each step depends on the chip, material and finish, so we quote it per program instead of publishing a ladder we would have to caveat. As a public anchor, a card near $0.35 at 500 pieces runs about $0.12-$0.18 at 50,000 pieces factory-direct — indicative only. Send the chip and the tiers you want priced (say 10K versus 100K) and you get an itemised quote within one business day.

faq.question: What is the lead time for a large RFID card run?
faq.answer: Blank cards from stock dispatch in 2-3 days. Custom printed and encoded runs are 5-7 days on the production line for orders from 1,000 to 1,000,000+ cards, then freight decides arrival: express 3-5 days for pilots, air 3-7 days, or sea 25-45 days for the pallet-scale balance. Annual programs pull against scheduled call-off, so the cards arrive as you need them rather than all at once.

faq.question: How are bulk RFID cards QC'd and packed for shipment?
faq.answer: Every encoded card gets a 100% functional read test at the line; first-piece and AQL sampling cover print and dimensional attributes, and out-of-spec lots are quarantined. A functional test report ships with the lot and batches stay traceable for seven years. Packing is to spec — bulk poly bag by default, or individual sleeves, retail blister or branded boxes — and we recommend 2-3% overage, supplied at cost, so field replacements never wait on a new run.

faq.question: Can I mix chip types in one bulk order?
faq.answer: Yes. Mixed-chip orders run at a 500-piece minimum per chip type in one production run — for example 5,000 MIFARE Classic 1K cards and 3,000 MIFARE DESFire cards on a single PO, each with its own artwork and encoding specification.

faq.question: Do you offer blanket orders and scheduled delivery for annual volume?
faq.answer: Yes. For annual supply agreements we produce the full-year quantity up front at the deep-tier price, hold it in our Shenzhen facility, and ship on scheduled call-off — monthly, quarterly or on demand, dispatched within 3-5 business days of release. You get bulk-tier pricing without warehousing the whole quantity yourself.
